name: Northern Yuan
summary: The Mongol state that continued on the steppe after the Yuan dynasty was driven out of China in 1368. Dayan Khan and Altan Khan revived its power; it ended when the Qing’s forerunners took it over in 1635.

knownFor.label: Altan Khan and the Dalai Lama title
knownFor.note: Altan Khan gave the title “Dalai Lama” to Sonam Gyatso.

location.value: At the height of Dayan Khan’s reign it stretched from the Siberian tundra and Lake Baikal in the north across the Gobi into the Ordos.

terrain.value: Grassy steppe, the Gobi Desert, the Khangai and Altai mountains, and the Ordos plateau inside the Yellow River bend.

climate.value: Strongly continental: long, very cold winters, short warm summers and little rain, especially in the Gobi.

resources.value: Herds of horses, sheep, cattle, goats and camels on wide pastures; grain, tea, silk and iron goods had to come from China.

disasters.value: Harsh winters (dzud) and droughts that killed herds, often pushing Mongols to raid or trade along the Ming border.

urbanisation.value: Mostly nomadic; a few towns such as Hohhot.

disease.value: Few records survive; smallpox was probably a serious danger, especially to Mongols visiting Chinese border towns.

migration.value: Mongols moved back to the steppe after 1368.

economicBase.value: The Ming reopened trade with the three Right Wing Tumens in 1571; a lack of trade drove repeated raids into China; the infobox lists barter and the dirham as currency.

tradeRoutes.value: Horse markets on the Ming frontier, opened after the 1571 peace with Altan Khan, where horses were traded for silk, tea, grain and iron goods.

wealth.value: Wealth was counted in herds; nobles also gained silk, silver and goods through Ming trade, tribute missions and raids.

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage of their own; nobles took livestock and labour from their herders, and trade with China was by barter or silver.

inequality.value: Genghisid nobles (taiji) ruled over commoner herders and servants; Buddhist lamas gained high status after 1578.

governmentType.value: A dynastic state ruled by the Mongol Borjigin clan, in which the Great Khan’s role became often only nominal.

keyRulers.value: Toghon Temür retreated north in 1368 and died at Yingchang in 1370; Biligtü ruled 1370–1378; Esen Taishi took the Yuan imperial title in 1453; Dayan Khan and Mandukhai reunited most Mongol tribes in the late 15th century; Ligdan Khan ruled 1604–1634. Sources differ on Esen: Wikipedia has him taking the imperial title in 1453 and dying in 1454; Seshat (citing Ishjamts) says he overthrew the khan in 1451 and was killed in 1455.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Northern Yuan (checked 13 Nov 2026); Seshat: Northern Yuan (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Seshat also names Tümen Jasaghtu (late 16th-century law code))

succession.value: Within the Genghisid line, often disputed.

institutions.value: Assemblies of nobles (khuraltai), the six tumens organised under Dayan Khan, and later Buddhist monasteries and law codes.

stability.value: Long periods of division between eastern Mongols and Oirats.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the eastern Mongols and the Oirats, whose leader Esen Taishi briefly took the khan’s title (1453), and quarrels among Genghisid princes.

armyAndTech.value: Mounted archers on steppe horses who raided across the Ming frontier; they had few firearms compared with the Ming and Manchus.

majorWars.value: The Ming sacked Karakorum in 1380; at the Tumu Crisis of 1449 Esen defeated a 500,000-strong Ming army and captured the Zhengtong Emperor.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Northern Yuan (checked 13 Nov 2026); Seshat: Northern Yuan (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Seshat confirms Esen captured the Ming emperor in 1449 with about 20,000 cavalry; it does not give the 500,000 Ming army figure and does not use the name Tumu)

territoryChange.value: Lost Inner Mongolia to the Later Jin (Qing) in 1635.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival of the Ming, which strengthened the Great Wall against Mongol raids; Altan Khan made peace with the Ming in 1571 and allied with Tibetan Buddhist leaders.

inventions.value: Few inventions are recorded; the Mongols kept steppe skills such as felt gers, composite bows and horse breeding.

openness.value: Open to trade with China and to Tibetan Buddhism, which Altan Khan adopted after meeting the Gelug leader Sonam Gyatso in 1578.

communicationTransport.value: Horses and camel caravans across the steppe and Gobi; trade roads ran to Ming border markets such as Datong and Zhangjiakou.

religion.value: Tengrism, Buddhism and Islam (infobox); Altan Khan and Sechen received the 3rd Dalai Lama in 1577 (the page says 1577, not 1578), beginning mass conversion to Tibetan Buddhism.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Northern Yuan (checked 13 Nov 2026); Seshat: Northern Yuan (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Seshat: largely shamanist before 1576, when Tümen Jasaghtu Khan and a Karma-pa lama made Tibetan Buddhism the state religion; the third Dalai Lama was received in 1577 (Ishjamts) or 1578 (Soucek), which is why the date stays disputed)

languageWriting.value: Mongolian, written in the Uyghur-derived Mongolian script; many Buddhist texts were translated, and the Kangyur was completed under Ligdan Khan.

artsArchitecture.value: Buddhist monasteries such as Erdene Zuu (1585) and the temples of Hohhot, Buddhist paintings and statues, and Mongol chronicles.

socialStructure.value: Genghisid nobles above commoner herders organised in clans and camp units, with servants and, later, a growing Buddhist clergy.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Mongol identity built on descent from Genghis Khan, the memory of the Yuan empire and, later, Tibetan Buddhism.

dailyLife.value: Families lived in felt gers and moved with the seasons, eating meat and dairy foods such as airag (fermented mare’s milk) and drinking tea.

neighbours.value: Ming China to the south, the Oirats to the west, Tibet to the southwest, the Jurchens (later Manchus) to the east, and Russia’s Siberia by the 1600s.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Tibetan Buddhism among the Mongols.

colonisation.value: Not colonised in this period; in 1635 the Chahar Mongols surrendered to the Later Jin, beginning Manchu rule over Inner Mongolia.

riseSignals.value: Dated from 1368, when the Ming took Dadu and Toghon Temür fled north; capitals Shangdu, Yingchang, then Karakorum (1371–1388).
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Northern Yuan (checked 13 Nov 2026); Seshat: Northern Yuan (checked 14 Nov 2026) (1368 retreat of Toghon Temür to Mongolia and Karakorum as capital match; Seshat says the Ming destroyed Karakorum in 1380)

peakPeriod.value: Dayan Khan reunited the Mongols from 1483 to 1510 and divided the realm among his sons; Esen Taishi (1438–1454) brought the Oirats to their height.

declineSignals.value: Long divisions between eastern Mongols and Oirats, Ligdan Khan’s failed attempt to reunite them, and the rise of the Manchus in the early 1600s.

outcome.value: Ligdan Khan (1604–1634) died in 1634; his son Ejei Khan surrendered the Imperial Seal to Hong Taiji in February 1635, ending Kublaid rule.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Northern Yuan (checked 13 Nov 2026); Seshat: Northern Yuan (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Seshat ends the Northern Yuan with Ligdan’s defeat by the Manchus in 1634 and has no Ejei date for 1635; the 1635 surrender stays Wikipedia-only)

overallCertainty.value: Mostly from Chinese and Mongolian chronicles.
